abstract.text: Applications in machine learning, optimization, and control require the sequential selection of a few system elements, such as sensors, data, or actuators, to optimize the system performance across multiple time steps. However, in failure-prone and adversarial environments, sensors get attacked, data get deleted, and actuators fail. Thence, traditional sequential design paradigms become insufficient and, in contrast, resilient sequential designs that adapt against system-wide attacks, deletions, or failures become important. In general, resilient sequential design problems are computationally hard. Also, even though they often involve objective functions that are monotone and (possibly) submodular, no scalable approximation algorithms are known for their solution. In this paper, we provide the first scalable algorithm, that achieves the following characteristics: system-wide resiliency, i.e., the algorithm is valid for any number of denial-of-service attacks, deletions, or failures; adaptiveness, i.e., at each time step, the algorithm selects system elements based on the history of inflicted attacks, deletions, or failures; and provable approximation performance, i.e., the algorithm guarantees for monotone objective functions a solution close to the optimal. We quantify the algorithm’s approximation performance using a notion of curvature for monotone (not necessarily submodular) set functions. Finally, we support our theoretical analyses with simulated experiments, by considering a control-aware sensor scheduling scenario, namely, sensing-constrained robot navigation.

thesis.text: The paper formalizes resilient monotone sequential maximization against worst-case attacks, deletions, or failures and gives the first adaptive algorithm with system-wide resiliency, minimal running time, and provable curvature-based approximation guarantees.

sections.summary: Motivates sequential selection under attacks and failures, then formalizes resilient monotone sequential maximization as a T-step max-min problem. The problem is interpreted as a perfect-information sequential game between a designer who selects sets and an attacker who removes elements after observing each selection.
sections.title: Introduction and Problem Formalization

sections.summary: Presents Algorithm 1, which constructs each selected set At as the union of two auxiliary sets. St,1 acts as bait by taking the βt highest-marginal elements, while St,2 greedily fills the remaining αt − βt elements while accounting for the history of realized removals.
sections.title: Adaptive Algorithm for Resilient Sequential Maximization

source_span.end_text: one-step version of Problem 1 where T = 1.

sections.summary: Defines curvature and total curvature for monotone set functions, then uses them to bound Algorithm 1's approximation performance. For monotone submodular functions the bound is (1 − κf)^4; for merely monotone functions it is (1 − cf)^5. Running time matches state-of-the-art non-resilient multi-step set-function optimization.
sections.title: Curvature and Performance Guarantees

source_span.end_text: the necessity for the resilient reformulation of the problem in eq. (1) per Problem 1 is exemplified.

sections.summary: Simulates sensing-constrained UAV navigation where the UAV selects 11 of 13 sensors under varying worst-case sensor failures. Algorithm 1 is compared with optimal brute force, random, and non-resilient greedy selection; it achieves at least 97% of optimal across tested scenarios, while greedy and random degrade as failures increase. The paper closes with future work on matroid constraints and applications.
sections.title: Numerical Experiments and Concluding Remarks

sections.summary: Supplies notation and preliminary lemmas used in the proof of Theorem 1. It covers curvature-based inequalities for monotone and submodular functions, the local greedy Algorithm 2, and Corollary 2 relating Algorithm 1's St,2 choices to an optimal non-resilient greedy benchmark.
sections.title: Appendix: Preliminary Lemmas and Greedy Guarantees

source_span.start_text: Lemma 7 Recall the notation in Theorem 1.

sections.summary: Proves Theorem 1. Lemma 7 connects the optimal non-resilient set Pt to the optimal resilient value. The approximation proofs chain the preliminary curvature inequalities to obtain the (1 − cf)^5 and (1 − κf)^4 bounds, and the running-time proof counts objective evaluations and sorting cost.
sections.title: Appendix: Proof of Theorem 1

sections.summary: Motivates sequential selection under attacks and failures, then formalizes resilient monotone sequential maximization as a T-step max-min problem. The problem is interpreted as a perfect-information sequential game between a designer who selects sets and an attacker who removes elements after observing each selection.
sections.title: Introduction and Problem Formalization

sections.summary: Presents Algorithm 1, which constructs each selected set At as the union of two auxiliary sets. St,1 acts as bait by taking the βt highest-marginal elements, while St,2 greedily fills the remaining αt − βt elements while accounting for the history of realized removals.
sections.title: Adaptive Algorithm for Resilient Sequential Maximization

source_span.end_text: one-step version of Problem 1 where T = 1.

sections.summary: Defines curvature and total curvature for monotone set functions, then uses them to bound Algorithm 1's approximation performance. For monotone submodular functions the bound is (1 − κf)^4; for merely monotone functions it is (1 − cf)^5. Running time matches state-of-the-art non-resilient multi-step set-function optimization.
sections.title: Curvature and Performance Guarantees

source_span.end_text: the necessity for the resilient reformulation of the problem in eq. (1) per Problem 1 is exemplified.

sections.summary: Simulates sensing-constrained UAV navigation where the UAV selects 11 of 13 sensors under varying worst-case sensor failures. Algorithm 1 is compared with optimal brute force, random, and non-resilient greedy selection; it achieves at least 97% of optimal across tested scenarios, while greedy and random degrade as failures increase. The paper closes with future work on matroid constraints and applications.

The approximation proofs chain the preliminary curvature inequalities to obtain the (1 − cf)^5 and (1 − κf)^4 bounds, and the running-time proof counts objective evaluations and sorting cost.
